title: Choose generic type parameters and constraints without replacing type safety with object casts

rubric.point: Explains that choosing IArchive<Invoice> binds both Save's parameter and Load's result to Invoice through the same type parameter.
Explains that saving an unrelated TemperatureReading through IArchive<Invoice> is rejected at compile time, whereas B accepts it at the method-call boundary.
Explains that A returns Invoice without a cast, whereas B requires a cast or runtime type check and can fail at runtime if the stored value has the wrong type.

questions.model:
With `IArchive<Invoice>`, the same type argument makes `Save` accept an `Invoice` and makes `Load` return an `Invoice`. The compiler rejects `Save(new TemperatureReading())` when `TemperatureReading` is unrelated to `Invoice`.

B accepts either object, so its signature cannot enforce an invoice-only archive. Its implementation must check that rule at runtime. Loading also returns only `object`; the caller must check or cast it. A cast to `Invoice` can fail at runtime if a different kind of item was stored. A preserves this type relationship in the API.

questions.prompt:
A method receives an existing value of type `T` and calls its `Describe()` method. That method is declared by `IDescribable`. Both classes and structs implement the interface, and the algorithm never constructs a `T`.

A developer proposes `where T : class, IDescribable, new()`. Explain which constraint the algorithm needs and why each additional constraint unnecessarily restricts callers. Why would removing all constraints and casting the value to `IDescribable` inside the method weaken the contract?

rubric.point: Identifies where T : IDescribable as sufficient and explains that it guarantees Describe is available to the generic implementation.
Explains that class unnecessarily excludes structs that implement IDescribable.
Explains that new() unnecessarily requires a public parameterless constructor because the algorithm receives an existing value and never constructs T.
Explains that an internal cast allows unsuitable type arguments through the public signature and moves detection to runtime, where the cast can fail.

questions.model:
The required constraint is `where T : IDescribable`. It guarantees that every permitted `T` supports `Describe()`, so the compiler allows the call without a cast.

`class` excludes valid struct implementations even though the algorithm needs no reference-type behavior. `new()` requires a public parameterless constructor even though the method never creates an instance; it can reject otherwise suitable classes.

With no constraint, callers can supply a type that does not implement `IDescribable`. Casting inside the method checks that requirement at runtime and can fail. The interface constraint states and enforces the requirement at compile time.

c1.feedback: You said you didn't know. The model answer shows what was needed.
